source_text: Si enim, quale tu, tale aliquid ille sensisset, debuit utique dicere: Per unius inoboedientiam peccatores constituti sunt omnes, sed per oboedientiam Christi ex his aliqui ad iustitiam reverterunt. Ita enim prorsus ei loquendum fuerat, si hoc, quod tu fingis, voluisset intellegi. Verumtamen cum hac sententia illud aliud nequivisset asserere multo magis profuisse Christi gratiam, quam Adae laesisset iniquitas. Etsi ergo penitus nesciremus, qui mos esset, quo per inoboedientiam unius hominis multi peccatores constitui dicerentur, tamen maneret in solido non hoc pertinere ad originale peccatum, quod Apostolus inculcaverat multis, non omnibus convenire.
pass_a_gloss: For if he had meant anything of such a kind as you, he ought certainly to have said: Through the disobedience of one all were constituted sinners, but through the obedience of Christ some from these returned unto justice. For so altogether he would have had to speak, if he had wanted this which you invent to be understood. Nevertheless with this sentence he would have been unable to assert that other thing, that the grace of Christ helped much more than Adam's iniquity had injured. Even if therefore we were inwardly ignorant what the custom was by which many were said to be constituted sinners through the disobedience of one human being, nevertheless it would remain on the solid that this does not belong to original sin, which the Apostle had stamped in as fitting many, not all.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: If he had meant anything like what you mean, he certainly ought to have said: ‘Through one man’s disobedience all were made sinners, but through Christ’s obedience some of these returned to righteousness.’ That is exactly how he should have spoken if he intended your invention to be understood. Yet with such a statement he could not also have asserted that Christ’s grace helped much more than Adam’s wickedness harmed. Even if, then, we had no idea at all what manner of conduct was meant by saying many were made sinners through one man’s disobedience, it would still remain firmly established that this does not concern original sin, since the apostle emphasized that it applies to many, not all (compare Romans 5:19).

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)
